title: Luke (18 October)
hook: the physician evangelist, patron of doctors and artists

segments.voice: Yesterday, Hedwig, the duchess who gave her wealth away to the poor. Your line was the duchess who gave. What did you give from what you had? Day one thousand thirty-seven.

Near the end of the letter to the Colossians, Paul passes on greetings from the people around him. Some get a name and little more. One gets a name and a job: "Luke the most dear physician." That's the man. A companion of Paul, a doctor, someone Paul was glad to have nearby. His name turns up a few times in Paul's letters, always briefly. And yet the Church's tradition puts his name on a whole Gospel and on the Acts of the Apostles. Doctors keep him as their patron. So do painters. Today's word is the evangelist with a doctor's eye.
screen: `A GREETING AT THE END OF A LETTER.` → `LUKE THE MOST DEAR PHYSICIAN.` → `DOCTORS AND PAINTERS CLAIM HIM.`

segments.voice: Start with how his Gospel begins. Before any angel, before any manger, the writer speaks to one person, a man named Theophilus. Others, he says, have set out to tell these things. He has looked into all of it carefully from the start, and now he will write it down in order, so Theophilus can be sure of what he was taught. That's not a poet clearing his throat. That's someone who checks. The Acts of the Apostles opens by speaking to the same Theophilus, which is why tradition reads the two books as one work in two parts, by one hand. Then the doctor's eye. Luke's Gospel is where you meet the good Samaritan bending over a beaten man on the road, pouring in oil and wine and binding up his wounds. It's where the prodigal son comes home hungry and the father runs. It's full of people at the edges: the sick, the poor, widows, outsiders. Some readers hear a physician in that, someone used to sitting with people in their worst week. Now the painters. Tradition says Luke painted Mary, and some old icons of her have been called his. Nobody can prove a brush was ever in his hand. But his first chapters are where Mary stands in full: the angel's greeting, the visit to Elizabeth, the birth, the shepherds. And then one quiet line: "But Mary kept all these words, pondering them in her heart." Whether or not he painted her, he gave artists their scenes.
screen: `WRITTEN IN ORDER, FOR THEOPHILUS.` · `ONE WORK IN TWO PARTS.` · `A DOCTOR'S EYE FOR THE WOUNDED.` · `HE GAVE PAINTERS THEIR SCENES.` · then, large: `MARY KEPT ALL THESE WORDS.`

segments.voice: Today's practice: draw something. Find a pen and the back of an envelope, a napkin, anything. Choose one thing in front of you, a cup, your own hand, a window. Settle, and breathe. Then draw it slowly, looking at it more than at the page. It doesn't need to be good. The point is to look at one thing long enough to see it, the way a doctor looks at a patient, the way Luke's pages linger on Mary. If you pray, you can offer the looking itself as a prayer. If you don't, just keep your eyes and your hand moving together for two minutes. The bell holds the time.
Luke. A companion of Paul, called the most dear physician, whom tradition names as the writer of a Gospel and of Acts, and the patron of doctors and artists.
Your line: the physician. Today, notice one person who is hurting a little, and give them a doctor's kind of attention: unhurried, close, and kind. Day one thousand thirty-seven.

howItsDone: Catholics keep the feast of Saint Luke on 18 October; doctors, nurses and artists often ask his prayers, and some hospitals and medical guilds bear his name.

notes: Audit (2026-10-01): 'comes home thin' changed to 'hungry' to match Luke 15:17; DR quotations (Col 4:14, Luke 2:19) checked; close-looking practice is near day 1041's plant practice, acceptable but noted.
Douay-Rheims wording to verify: Colossians 4:14 'Luke the most dear physician' and Luke 2:19 'But Mary kept all these words, pondering them in her heart.'
Authorship of Luke and Acts is attributed to tradition, not stated as fact; neither book names its author.
'His name turns up a few times in Paul's letters' (Col 4:14, 2 Tim 4:11, Philemon 24); confirm the phrasing.
'Some readers hear a physician' in Luke's attention to the sick and outsiders: framed as a reading, not a fact.
The painter tradition (icons attributed to Luke) is given as tradition with 'nobody can prove' it; confirm the Keeper is comfortable with that framing.
Feast date 18 October appears only in the title and howItsDone.
Editor: practice no longer claims Luke looked at Mary in person; it now refers to how his Gospel lingers on her.
